title: Violin Concerto
hook: A concerto in the classical European mould that ends with a dance from the Black Sea coast.

painting.title: Istanbul
painting.pairingNote: A coffee house on the shore of the Bosphorus, painted by one of the first Turkish painters to work in the European manner; Erkin, born in the city, joined European form and Turkish music in the same spirit.

facts: Ulvi Cemal Erkin (1906–1972) was one of the “Turkish Five”, the first generation of composers of the Turkish Republic. All five trained in Europe and set out to join its forms with the melodies and rhythms of Turkish music. He wrote the Violin Concerto in 1946–47, after his dance rhapsody *Köçekçe* and his First Symphony.

A premiere planned for a festival in Vienna in 1947 did not take place. The concerto was first heard on 2 April 1948, on the opening night of Ankara’s new opera house, with the Presidential Symphony Orchestra and the violinist Licco Amar. Born in Budapest, Amar had led Paul Hindemith’s string quartet in Germany and had taught in Ankara since leaving Nazi Germany.

The plan is the classical one: a first movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with a [[cadenza|cadenza]], a slow movement in three parts and a [[rondo|rondo]] to finish. The Turkish colour is in the melodies and rhythms. The first theme leans on a Turkish [[makam|makam]], the second sounds more Anatolian still, and the finale is a horon, the fast dance of the Black Sea coast, with a passage in the spirit of a [[taksim|taksim]].

It is a soloist’s concerto, with long lines to sing and passages that test the player’s technique. The slow movement stands apart: its lines interweave rather than sing over an accompaniment, and one analyst hears the Baroque in it.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a serious, broad first movement with a cadenza at its heart (I), a song over a slow, plucked tread (II), a fast Black Sea dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro giusto
movements.summary: The longest movement, about half the concerto. After a roll on the timpani, violin and orchestra set out a serious, broad theme; a second theme with a more Turkish turn follows. In the middle the violin plays a long cadenza alone, and the movement ends with a weighty, decisive [[coda|coda]]. Its form is close to a textbook [[sonata-form|sonata form]].

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, earnest
mainIdeas.description: a broad melody for violin and orchestra that climbs on rising scales. Its repeated, step-by-step phrases lean on the Kürdi [[makam|makam]].

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, Anatolian
mainIdeas.description: a contrasting tune whose melody and rhythm are closer to Turkish folk music, shared between the violin and the woodwind.

stops.hear: A quiet passage in the orchestra, with an ardent line in the violin; then heavy, decisive closing bars

notice: Listen for where the cadenza falls. In most concertos it comes near the end; here it sits in the middle of the movement, and the orchestra still has a long way to go after it.
Compare the two themes. The first could almost come from a European concerto of the 1930s; the second sounds closer to Anatolia.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: James Buswell, an American violinist, recorded the concerto in Istanbul in November 2014 with the Istanbul State Symphony Orchestra, whose roots go back to the city orchestra founded by Cemal Reşit Rey, another of the Turkish Five. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 2–4, between *Köçekçe* and Erkin’s Second Symphony.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A slow movement in three parts: a long melody, a middle section that climbs in steps, and the melody again. Under the strings’ steady, thoughtful theme the basses pluck a slow, even tread that hardly stops. The violin does not simply sing over an accompaniment: its line is woven in with the others, and Metin Munzur of the Ankara State Conservatory hears something of the Baroque in it.

mainIdeas.name: The tread
mainIdeas.description: plucked notes in the basses, walking at an even pace ([[pizzicato|pizzicato]]).

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, grave melody in the strings, later taken up by the violin, with a melancholy that the woodwind deepen.

stops.hear: The strings play a steady, thoughtful melody; underneath, the basses pluck even, walking notes
Woodwind join in; the colour turns wistful
The violin weaves the melancholy theme through the orchestra; the lines rub against one another
stops.happening: The first part unfolds, line against line, in [[counterpoint|counterpoint]]

stops.hear: A short phrase is repeated, each time a step higher or lower; the music grows more urgent
stops.happening: The middle part, built on sequences

stops.hear: The opening melody returns

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The melody’s last phrase; the plucked tread still walks underneath

notice: Follow the plucked basses. They keep the slow pulse almost from the first bar to the last.
Notice how often the violin is one voice among several, rather than the singer with an accompaniment.

movements.heading: Allegro con fuoco
movements.summary: “Fast, with fire.” The finale is a horon, the quick, driving dance of the Black Sea coast, set as a [[rondo|rondo]]: the dance tune keeps coming back between contrasting episodes. It is the most openly Turkish of the three movements. The violin plays crisp [[double-stop|double stop]]s against a pounding orchestra, and before the end a free, unmeasured passage recalls the [[taksim|taksim]] of Turkish violinists.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a fast, insistent dance tune, with short, repeated figures.

mainIdeas.name: The episodes
mainIdeas.description: contrasting tunes between the returns of the refrain, some built from short phrases repeated at new pitches.

stops.hear: A fast, driving tune; the violin plays crisp double stops over a pounding orchestra
A different tune, in a new colour
The dance tune returns
A longer contrasting section; short phrases are passed around and repeated at rising pitches; fine woodwind solos
The dance tune again, as driving as ever
The first episode’s tune comes back

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The beat stops; the violin plays alone, freely, as if improvising
stops.happening: A passage in the spirit of a [[taksim|taksim]]

stops.label: Last 25 seconds
stops.hear: The dance returns at full speed and runs to a loud close

notice: Count how many times the dance tune comes back. Each return is a little landmark in the rondo.

In the free violin passage near the end, the pulse disappears. In Turkish music a taksim is an improvisation played before or within a piece; here it is written out, but it is meant to sound improvised.

threads.title: Two traditions
threads.body: The form of every movement is European: sonata form, a three-part slow movement, a rondo. The colour comes from Turkish music: a makam in the first theme, an Anatolian second theme, a horon and a taksim in the finale.

threads.title: The violin’s long road
threads.body: The concerto gives the soloist room to sing and to dazzle. Licco Amar played it first, in Ankara in 1948; ten years later the Turkish violinist Ayla Erduran played it in Brussels, with Erkin conducting.

threads.title: Ankara
threads.body: Erkin taught in Ankara for more than forty years, and the concerto was heard first on the night the city’s opera house opened.
